draft.title: Relative frequency and trials
card: A trial is one go at an experiment, such as one coin toss. Doing many trials and recording the results is how we test chance.
Relative frequency is how often an outcome happened, divided by the number of trials. Relative frequency \(=\) number of times it happened \(\div\) number of trials.
Example: Sam tosses a coin 20 times and gets 12 heads. The relative frequency of heads is \(\frac{12}{20} = 0.6\).
The theoretical probability of heads is \(0.5\). With more trials, relative frequency usually gets closer to this, but it may not match it exactly.
draft.remember: Relative frequency is times it happened over trials, and it usually nears the probability as trials grow.

a.q: Priya rolls a die 40 times and gets a six 8 times. What is the relative frequency of a six?
a.why: Relative frequency is the number of sixes over the number of trials, so \(\frac{8}{40} = 0.2\). The value \(\frac{1}{6}\) is the theoretical probability, not what happened in her trials.
a.clue: Divide how often it happened by the number of trials.

b.q: Leo tosses a coin and records heads each time. Which of his results will most likely be closest to 0.5 for heads?
b.why: 300 in 600 is exactly 0.5, and with so many trials it is the most likely to be near 0.5. Small numbers of tosses can land near 0.5 by luck, as 1 in 2 does, but they are less reliable.
b.clue: More trials usually give a more reliable result.

problems.detail: The question asks which recorded result 'will most likely be' closest to 0.5, but the results are already given. '1 head in 2 tosses' is exactly 0.5, just like 300 in 600, so two options are equally close and a careful student could defend either. Reword it to ask which result Leo should trust most as an estimate, or change 1 in 2 so it is not exactly 0.5.
The why says 1 in 2 lands 'near 0.5 by luck', but it is exactly 0.5. This understates the problem that two options are equally correct as written.

proposal.title: Relative frequency and trials
card: A trial is one go at an experiment, such as one coin toss. Doing many trials and recording the results is how we test chance.
Relative frequency is how often an outcome happened, divided by the number of trials. Relative frequency \(=\) number of times it happened \(\div\) number of trials.
Example: Sam tosses a coin 20 times and gets 12 heads. The relative frequency of heads is \(\frac{12}{20} = 0.6\).
The theoretical probability of heads is \(0.5\). With more trials, relative frequency usually gets closer to it, so results from many trials give a more reliable estimate than results from a few.
proposal.remember: Relative frequency is times it happened over trials. More trials usually give a better estimate of the probability.

a.q: Priya rolls a die 40 times and gets a six 8 times. What is the relative frequency of a six?
a.why: Relative frequency is the number of sixes over the number of trials, so \(\frac{8}{40} = 0.2\). The value \(\frac{1}{6}\) is the theoretical probability, not what happened in her trials.
a.clue: Divide how often it happened by the number of trials.

b.q: Leo tosses the same coin in four separate sets and records the heads. Which set gives the most reliable estimate of the probability of heads?
b.why: The set of 600 tosses has by far the most trials, so its relative frequency, \(\frac{290}{600} \approx 0.48\), is the most reliable estimate. The set of 2 tosses gives exactly \(0.5\), but with only two trials that match is down to luck, so it is not reliable.
b.clue: Look at the number of trials, not just the answer.
